outline.description: Sets out who the petitioners are, the timeline of events in Colombia that led to their departure, their limited interactions with law enforcement, and the course of the immigration proceedings through the IJ, the BIA, and this appeal. Identifies exactly what issues are preserved for appellate review.
subtopics: Petitioners’ identities and background: Colombian family from Bogotá; furniture factory owners; Jimenez’s provisional law license and prosecutorial internship
Political activity: Liberal Party membership since 2012; campaigning for Federico Gutiérrez in 2022; generalized threats to party members

Property-dispute entanglement: client’s request to approach tenant/ex-husband; discovery that tenant is “Don Rafa,” a narco-guerrilla leader; property’s criminal uses; prior law-enforcement searches; police warning to stay away

Escalating incidents: threatening brochure (“death to snitches from Liberal Party”); armed men at factory telling Jimenez to leave; assault on employee demanding petitioners’ whereabouts; school incident involving younger son
Limited police contact and decision to flee: advice from officers to avoid trouble/leave; brief relocation to countryside; departure to the U.S.
Removal proceedings: NTAs; concessions to removability; IJ’s credibility finding but denials (no persecution, no nexus, government protection not shown, internal relocation feasible; CAT denied)
BIA affirmance: single-member decision; due process/counsel claim rejected; issues preserved on petition for review limited to asylum and withholding (no CAT or due process challenges)

outline.chapter_title: Appellate Scope, Burdens, and Governing Doctrines
outline.description: Explains the court’s jurisdiction, scope and standard of review, and the substantive asylum/withholding framework that structures the analysis, including the elements of past persecution, nexus to a protected ground, state action or inability/unwillingness to protect, future fear, and internal relocation.
subtopics: Jurisdiction under 8 U.S.C. § 1252 and record-based review; consolidated review of asylum claims
Standard of review: substantial evidence; deference unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude otherwise
Review focus on BIA with reference to IJ’s reasoning when helpful
Asylum eligibility: refugee definition; applicant’s burden by preponderance of evidence
Past persecution pathway: (1) severity of harm, (2) nexus to protected ground, (3) government involvement or inability/unwillingness to control
Presumption of future fear from established past persecution and how it may be rebutted
Withholding of removal: higher standard than asylum; dependency on failing/succeeding asylum elements
Nexus doctrine: “at least one central reason” and mixed-motive analysis
Government protection test: reporting/notice, efforts to stop persecutors, protective measures; futility/danger exceptions
Internal relocation: feasibility and reasonableness as an alternative ground to deny relief

outline.chapter_title: Past Persecution: Threats and Psychological Harm Do Not Suffice Here
outline.description: Assesses whether the cumulative incidents rise to the level of persecution. Applies Tenth Circuit precedent that threats alone, and psychological/emotional distress absent severe accompanying conduct, generally do not meet the persecution threshold.
subtopics: Persecution concept: must entail more than restrictions or threats to life and liberty; cumulative assessment of incidents
Record evidence: multiple threats, armed confrontations, employee assault, school incident; petitioners’ concession of no lasting physical harm
Threats alone are insufficient; physical injury not required but harm must be severe and offensive
Psychological and emotional effects (insomnia, panic attacks) considered but found inadequate without qualifying severity
Comparator cases illustrating higher-severity fact patterns still found insufficient (e.g., Karki; Brandy; Chhetri; Carias-Mejia)
Conclusion: substantial evidence supports BIA/IJ finding that aggregate harm does not constitute past persecution

outline.chapter_title: Nexus to a Protected Ground: Criminal Retaliation, Not Political Opinion
outline.description: Analyzes whether petitioners showed that political opinion was at least one central reason for the harm. Concludes the record supports a non-political, criminal-protection motive tied to Jimenez’s interference with Don Rafa’s enterprise, and notes the unbriefed PSG claim.
subtopics: Protected grounds asserted: political opinion; particular social group not meaningfully briefed (forfeited)
Temporal and causal sequence: escalation after property dispute and investigative interest in Don Rafa’s property
Statements evidencing motive: accusations of being a “snitch” for the prosecutor’s office/police; blame for searches/seizures at the property
Lack of evidence linking early political threats to Don Rafa; petitioners continued political campaigning undeterred at that time
Mixed-motive framework: protected ground must be a central reason, not incidental or subordinate
Holding on nexus: substantial evidence supports that criminal retaliation/self-protection was the predominant motive; political opinion was tangential

outline.chapter_title: Government Protection, Internal Relocation, and Disposition
outline.description: Evaluates whether the Colombian government was unable or unwilling to protect petitioners and whether safe internal relocation was reasonable. Concludes the record does not show systemic government failure or futility of reporting, and that relocation within Colombia is feasible. States the final outcome and practical implications.
subtopics: Reporting and notice: minimal outreach (conversations with two officers); absence of formal complaints or escalation through available contacts
Isolated officer comments versus systemic failure: limited probative value of one-off apathy; need for evidence of broader inability/unwillingness
Countervailing evidence of enforcement: prior searches/seizures targeting the property undermine claims of government collusion
Futility/danger exception: record does not substantiate that reporting would have been futile or dangerous
Internal relocation indicators: safe three-week stay in countryside; family remains unharmed in Colombia; threats focused on leaving the neighborhood, not the country
Alternative holding: even assuming future fear, relocation is reasonable and feasible
Disposition: petition for review denied; asylum ineligible; withholding necessarily fails due to higher burden
Practice takeaways: document severe harm beyond threats; build evidence of nexus; create a record of reporting or credible futility; address relocation with concrete, country-specific obstacles
